name: CT-RATE
description: A public dataset pairing non-contrast 3D chest CT volumes with corresponding radiology text reports. CT-RATE comprises 25,692 scans from 21,304 unique patients and 50,188 reconstructed 3D chest CT volumes, with each exam accompanied by a report including findings and impression sections. The dataset is used to develop CT-CLIP and CT-CHAT.
creator: Ibrahim Ethem Hamamci, Sezgin Er, Chenyu Wang, Furkan Almas, Ayse Gulnihan Simsek, Sewal Nil Esirgun, Irem Dogan, Omer Faruk Durugol, Benjamin Hou, Suprosanna Shit, Weicheng Dai, Murong Xu, Hadrien Reynaud, Muhammed Furkan Dasdelen, Bastian Wittmann, Tamaz Amiranashvili, Enis Simsar, Mehmet Simsar, Emine Bensu Erdemir, Abdullah Alanbay, Anjany Sekuboyina, Berkan Lafci, Ahmet Kaplan, Zhiyong Lu, Malgorzata Polacin, Bemhard Kainz, Christian Bluethgen, Kayhan Batmanghelich, Mehmet Kemal Ozdemir, and Bjoem Menze
citeAs: Ibrahim Ethem Hamamci. CT-RATE: Paired chest CT volumes and radiology reports. https://huggingface.co/datasets/ibrahimhamamci/CT-RATE. 2025.
rai:dataCollection: We curate a novel dataset, CT-RATE, consisting of chest CT volumes and corresponding radiology text reports from Istanbul Medipol University Mega Hospital. The dataset includes non-contrast chest CT volumes acquired between May 2015 and January 2023, totaling 50,188 reconstructed CT volumes from 25,692 distinct CT experiments conducted on 21,304 unique patients. In clinical practice, CT volumes are reconstructed with various techniques for specific diagnostic requirements, and the authors incorporate every reconstructed volume from the hospital database into the dataset. Reports are structured into four sections: clinical information, technique, findings, and impression.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data are chest CT volumes and corresponding radiology text reports from Istanbul Medipol University Mega Hospital. The CT-RATE dataset contains the original raw data. Each chest CT exam is accompanied by a report authored by a radiologist, and anonymized metadata are also included.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: To anonymize the CT-RATE dataset, the authors first anonymize reports by removing all personal information pertaining to patients and medical professionals using targeted searches with regular expressions to identify and eliminate date-related information and patient-doctor identifiers. The anonymized reports are then translated from Turkish to English using the Google Translate API, and bilingual final-year medical students review and correct all translations, remove any residual personal information, and ensure coherence. For CT volumes, they exclude volumes that involve contrast material or body parts other than the chest, standardize orientation by examining metadata, and remove all identifying information from the metadata.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Each volume is resized to achieve uniform spacing of 0.75 mm in the x-axis and y-axis and 1.5 mm in the z-axis. The CT volumes are then either center-cropped or padded to reach a consistent resolution of 480 × 480 × 240. Subsequently, the authors convert each CT volume to Hounsfield Unit values using intercept and slope values from the metadata. HU values are clipped to a range of -1000 to 1000, and during training these values are normalized to a range of -1 to 1. Identical preprocessing methods are applied to the external datasets for consistent evaluation.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Each volume is annotated with 18 abnormalities for validation and fine-tuning. To develop an automated label extractor model, the authors manually annotate 1,000 reports by merging findings and impression sections to create a multi-label dataset identifying 18 abnormalities. Conditions not referenced in either section are considered absent. Similar conditions are grouped, such as left and right mucoid impactions under mucoid impaction, various lung opacities under lung opacity, and lung and fissural nodules under lung nodules. The annotated reports are divided into training (800 reports) and validation (200 reports) sets. They then finetune the RadBERT-RoBERTa-4m model and apply it to classify the remaining 24,692 reports. In addition, organ-level anatomical segmentation labels are generated using a state-of-the-art segmentation model, and over 2.7 million question-answer pairs for CT-CHAT are derived from CT-RATE using Llama 3.1 8B and rule-based methods.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Google Translate API, Hugging Face, GitHub
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The authors report precision, recall, and F1 scores for the finetuned text encoder used for automatic label extraction, showing robust classification across abnormalities. They merge findings and impression sections because some abnormalities are not explicitly mentioned in a single section. Since the VQA dataset is generated by a large language model, they carefully select only accurately generated and properly formatted data, specifically data that can be successfully parsed as JSON for training.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Bilingual final-year medical students reviewed and corrected all report translations, removed residual personal information, and ensured coherence. Expert evaluations of CT-CHAT report generation were conducted by three board-certified radiologists; two were board-certified thoracic radiologists from Zurich and one was from Istanbul.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: RadBERT-RoBERTa-4m, Google Translate API, Llama 3.1 8B, Llama 3.1 7B, TotalSegmentator
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is publicly accessible via Hugging Face, and trained models and codebases are publicly available on GitHub. The authors state that they plan to extend CT-RATE with multi-abnormality segmentation and localization labels for 3D chest CT volumes as future work.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Patient age, patient sex, clinical information in reports, medical history, symptoms, metadata including StudyDate before anonymization, and geography/institution source. The authors state that they anonymize all chest CT volumes, associated metadata, and radiology text reports before computational analysis.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The open-source release of CT-RATE, CT-CLIP, and CT-CHAT addresses critical challenges in 3D medical imaging and lays the groundwork for future innovations in medical AI and improved patient care. The models are described as potentially reducing radiologists' workload, enhancing workflows, improving diagnostic accuracy, and broadening accessibility through a user-friendly graphical interface for educational and clinical research settings.
rai:dataBiases: The authors state that biases inherent to their single-institution dataset may influence self-supervised training. Although they curate a large and diverse set of volume-report pairs, the data originates from a single geographic and clinical setting, which may limit generalizability to other populations. They also note that CT-CLIP depends on the specific terminology used in reports and the choice of prompts during zero-shot detection, and variability in how diseases are described across radiology reports can affect detection accuracy.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is single-center and may have limited generalizability to other populations. Detailed metadata for the second external validation set are not publicly available. CT-CLIP depends on report terminology and prompt choice. The evaluation of CT-CHAT is limited by the lack of pretrained 3D medical multimodal AI assistants for benchmarking, so comparisons are made against 2D models using DRRs. The quality of generated reports remains insufficient for clinical use, and the models remain far from ready for clinical deployment. Current models are limited to chest CT volumes and do not cover other modalities or anatomical regions.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is used for training and internal validation of CT-CLIP and CT-CHAT, for zero-shot multi-abnormality detection, finetuning, volume-to-volume retrieval, report-to-volume retrieval, visual question answering, and report generation. CT-RATE is divided into training and internal validation sets for experiments, with 20,000 patients allocated to training and 1,304 for validation. The authors also state that organ-level anatomical segmentation labels may support tasks such as visual grounding and anatomical localization.
